summary:
Sachsen-Anhalt stands under the German national framework: federal constitutional and equality protections apply in every Land, national identity documents and marriage law are uniform, and no Land can remove that floor. Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several Länder have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all.

The exceptional-case rule was applied against a legally recognised woman in the case that now drives federal politics. Marla-Svenja Liebich was sentenced in July 2023 by the Halle District Court in Saxony-Anhalt to 18 months' imprisonment without parole for incitement to hatred, defamation and insult, and changed her legal gender from male to female by declaration at a registry office under the Self-Determination Act at the end of 2024. In August 2025 the chief public prosecutor in Halle told MDR Sachsen-Anhalt that she would begin the term at Chemnitz women's prison. After her extradition from the Czech Republic in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison at Zeithain, in the Meissen district, with prison management stating that the decision prioritised the safety of women at the Chemnitz facility, and a court has yet to decide whether the gender changes can be reversed.

Sachsen-Anhalt is one of three partner Länder, with Sachsen and Thüringen, in a Bundesrat initiative reported on 2 June 2026 to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act. The proposal would add an "abuse review" mechanism giving registry offices objective, documentable grounds to intervene, and its sponsors cite the Fall Liebich. It is backed by Union MPs, resisted by SPD ministers, and runs alongside a scheduled evaluation of the Self-Determination Act being run by the federal family ministry.

Screening is a documented flashpoint at ports of entry. In June 2025 the DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which officers allegedly deliberately disregarded her gender identity; she characterised the incident as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment and gave Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport. Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025: a Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a debate about registered trans women's access, in which trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic.

Reporting and support machinery exists for hostility encountered in country. The STOP the HATE campaign site, run by the Prevention and Empowerment organisation in northern Germany, provides a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.
tangentialFactors:
Reporting on the limits of the custody exception predates the Liebich transfer. DW reported on 23 August 2023 that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates, a finding illustrated by the case of climate activist Penelope Frank of Last Generation, legally recorded male, who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted.

The Liebich case has drawn sustained editorial hostility toward the self-declaration route itself, with German outlets including Der Spiegel questioning the seriousness of her gender change. Her own far-right record is part of the political framing: she organised demonstrations from 2014 onward, many on Halle's central market square, and was arrested in the Czech Republic in April 2026.

Support and facility practice vary by Land. The Berlin prison service maintains an official page in German with information and contacts for trans, inter and non-binary persons held across the city's facilities, and Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel reported on how Berlin saunas and similar venues now treat trans women after months of public argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused. Comparable statutory change is visible in Rhineland-Palatinate, whose § 17 took effect on 1 March 2026 without press coverage.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change for residents runs through the declaration route at a registry office under the Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 January 2025, and Liebich used that route at the end of 2024. Whether a completed change can be undone is unresolved: a court has yet to decide whether her changes can be reversed, so the standing of a registry declaration is not settled in German law.

Residents are directly exposed to the outcome of the Bundesrat initiative. It is an attempt by Sachsen-Anhalt with Sachsen and Thüringen, not a change in the law: the proposal is backed by opposition lawmakers and resisted by governing-party ministers, and it runs against a scheduled federal evaluation of the Self-Determination Act being conducted by the federal family ministry.

Prison placement for residents follows the same binary men and women housing model that governs the custody exception for visitors, with placement matching gender identity practised only exceptionally under the reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act used by the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records how the Sachsen-Anhalt prison administration itself handles intake placement for a legally recognised trans person, or whether the Land has issued internal guidance following the Chemnitz-to-Zeithain transfer. That is unresolved and not sourced here.

Whether the proposed abuse review mechanism will be adopted is unresolved: the initiative is a proposal before the Bundesrat, opposed by SPD ministers, with a federal evaluation of the Self-Determination Act still running.

Whether Marla-Svenja Liebich's gender change will stand is unresolved; a court has yet to decide whether the changes can be reversed, and no outcome is sourced.

Whether Sachsen-Anhalt maintains a public contact page or guidance for trans, inter and non-binary detainees comparable to Berlin's is not sourced in this inventory.
